what_it_does: Every modern processor keeps a Branch Target Buffer (BTB), which is essentially a small table that remembers where a branch instruction (an 'if' or 'jump' in a program) is likely to send execution next, so the processor can speculatively start work there before confirming. Researchers have shown that attackers can spy on a victim program by watching how their own BTB lookups are slowed when they collide with the victim's entries — or actively mislead the victim's processor by poisoning those entries. This paper proposes CryptoBTB, which encrypts the index used to look up BTB entries so that one program's entries are stored in a different location than another program's entries for the same address, preventing collisions across privilege levels or between processes. To avoid making branch prediction slower, the encryption is done on a path that is not in the critical timing path of the prediction. The design also uses two levels of BTB (a small fast one and a larger slower one) to handle programs with large code footprints better than prior encrypted designs.
